title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
hints: a sorted array is already an inorder traversal of a valid BST - any element can be the root as long as everything before it goes left and everything after it goes right
to keep the tree height-balanced, the root of each slice should split the remaining elements into two halves of nearly equal size
write a helper that takes a (lo, hi) index range into nums and returns the subtree built from that range, recursing on (lo, mid-1) and (mid+1, hi)
since even-length slices have two valid middle candidates, this problem fixes the tiebreak: always take the lower-index one, floor((lo+hi)/2)
place each constructed value directly at its computed heap index in a growable output array, rather than building a linked structure and converting afterward
commonMistakes: picking the higher-index middle for even-length slices instead of the lower-index one specified here, which produces a different (still valid but non-matching) tree
off-by-one errors in the (lo, hi) slice boundaries, causing elements to be dropped or duplicated
forgetting the array can encode a tree taller than a simple full binary tree once heap indices are computed, and under-allocating the output array

content.problemStatement:
Binary trees in these problems are encoded as a flat array named `tree`
using complete-binary-tree (heap) indexing:

- the root sits at index 0
- a node at index `i` has its left child at index `2*i+1` and right child at index `2*i+2`
- any position at or beyond the end of the array, or holding the sentinel value `-101`, means "no node there"
- real node values are always in the range -100 to 100, so -101 can never be mistaken for a genuine value

You're given an array of distinct integers, `nums`, sorted in strictly
ascending order.

**Build a height-balanced binary search tree containing exactly those values, and return it using the flat array encoding described above.**

Height-balanced means that for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Multiple height-balanced trees can exist for the same input, so use this deterministic rule to pick one: the root of any slice is always the element at the slice's lower-index middle position (for a slice of even length n, that's index floor((n-1)/2) within the slice, the left one of the two middle candidates), with everything before it forming the left subtree and everything after it forming the right subtree, recursively.
constraints: nums is sorted in strictly ascending order with no duplicates
notes: a two-element array, where the lower-index-middle tiebreak rule matters
an array whose length is a power of two minus one, producing a perfectly balanced tree

sampleTestCases.explanation: the middle of 5 elements is index 2 (value 0), which becomes the root; [-10, -3] becomes the left subtree and [5, 9] becomes the right subtree, each split the same way
a slice of 2 elements picks the lower-index middle, index 0 (value 1), as the root, leaving 3 as its right child with no left child
a single element is its own root with no children

optimal.time: O(n), visiting each element once to place it
optimal.space: O(log n) for the recursion stack (the tree is height-balanced by construction), plus O(n) for the output array
optimal.pattern: divide and conquer: recursively pick the lower-index middle of each slice as that subtree's root

bruteForce.approach: there isn't a separate brute force here - the natural recursive definition (pick the slice's lower-index middle element as root, recurse on the two halves) already is the intended solution
